The premise isn't right: more agents don't always give better results. Neither five nor ten is a good starting point.

**Why it's tempting:** a team of specialists works well for people, because each person does the task in parallel with their own skills. Agents differ in two ways. Each one is a separate loop of model calls, and each one starts with only the text you hand it. So every extra agent adds cost, and every handoff between agents can lose information.

**Example:** a student asks, "Is the laser cutter free Friday, and what settings for 3 mm acrylic?" One agent handles this in a few steps: check the calendar, search the manual, answer. With ten agents (calendar, manual, booking, router, checker and so on), a router agent reads the question, passes it on, and each specialist re-reads its piece. You pay for more model calls and more repeated context, and the answer is often no better. A detail like "Friday" can also get dropped in a handoff.

**When splitting pays off:**
- One agent's context gets overloaded, for example by very long manual excerpts that other steps don't need.
- Tasks are independent and can run in parallel.
- Parts need different tools or permissions, such as keeping booking write access away from the manual Q&A.

Your assistant has a small budget and short, sequential requests, so the sensible design is one agent with three tools. Add a second agent only if you can name which of those three reasons applies.

Quick check: which of those three reasons, if any, would justify a separate agent for searching the long manuals?
